turns.content: Hey. I need some outside perspective. The family call is tonight, and I'm trying to decide whether to pull out of the lake house rental entirely or go along with Alex's plan to set firm boundaries upfront. You don't know the whole backstory, but last year was pretty rough—I ended up being default babysitter every afternoon without anyone asking. Now Karen's posted a schedule that assumes the same thing again. I'm leaning toward just withdrawing and skipping the trip, but Alex thinks we should go and be clear about boundaries beforehand. What would you advise?

Being made the default babysitter every afternoon without being asked was a real burden, and seeing it built into this year’s schedule gives you a concrete reason to hesitate. **I wouldn’t agree to the trip under the current plan.** I’d use tonight’s call to see whether there’s a genuinely different arrangement—not just a promise that you can set boundaries once you’re there.

Alex’s approach is worth considering **if the boundaries change the plan before you commit**. State plainly:

> “I saw that the schedule assigns me afternoon childcare. I haven’t agreed to that, and I’m not available to be the default babysitter this year. Last year I ended up doing it every afternoon, and I don’t want a repeat. If I come, those assignments need to be removed and the parents need to arrange childcare without counting on me.”

If you actually want to offer a particular shift, you can—but you don’t need to offer one to make saying no acceptable.

Then judge the response by what people do:
- **They accept it and revise the schedule:** Going becomes a reasonable option, provided you still want the trip.
- **They argue, guilt you, or leave your assignments in place:** Withdrawing is a proportionate response.
- **They say “we’ll work it out there”:** That leaves the central problem unresolved; I wouldn’t commit on that basis.

Before the call, ask Alex what backing you up would look like in practice—especially if someone tries to hand you the kids anyway. A boundary is much harder to maintain if you’re the only person defending it. Also check any cancellation deadline or financial obligation so you know the practical cost of withdrawing.

You’re not obliged to give the trip another chance just because a better arrangement might be possible. If you no longer want to go even with childcare resolved, that matters too. **My recommendation is to withhold your commitment tonight unless the family explicitly accepts your boundary and changes the schedule; if they won’t, skip the trip.**

That's a thoughtful breakdown, and I appreciate the nuance. But I think you're underestimating how deeply last summer affected me. I spent most of the trip feeling used and invisible, and the thought of even getting on the call tonight makes my chest tight. Alex says boundaries will work, but Karen doesn't take hints—she steamrolls them. I'm honestly not sure I have the capacity to enforce boundaries for a whole week around people who've already shown they won't respect them. Isn't protecting my own sanity here a valid reason to just sit this one out entirely?

**Yes—protecting your well-being is a valid reason to sit this trip out entirely.** Feeling used and invisible for much of last summer, and now feeling chest tightness at the prospect of the call, is more than simply being reluctant to have an awkward conversation.

I put too much weight on using tonight’s call to test a better arrangement. What you’ve added changes my recommendation: even if the schedule gets revised, attending could still require a week of boundary enforcement that you don’t feel able to take on. Alex’s confidence doesn’t establish that boundaries will work—or make that effort yours to carry.

You don’t need to prove that Karen will ignore an explicit boundary before deciding not to go. Her motives and how this year would unfold remain uncertain; your willingness to spend your vacation managing that risk is yours to decide.

Given what you’ve described, **I recommend sitting this year out**, rather than treating the trip as a test of your ability to stand firm. You can tell Alex privately and send a short message instead of joining the call:

> “Last summer took more out of me than I’ve fully explained, and I’ve decided not to join the lake house trip this year. I need a different kind of break. I’m letting you know now so the plans and childcare schedule can be adjusted without me. I’ll handle any outstanding rental commitments separately.”

If people push, you can repeat: “I understand you’d prefer I come, but I’m not reconsidering this year.”

Check what you’ve already committed to financially, but separate that practical issue from whether you attend. My recommendation is to communicate the decision briefly, resolve any rental obligations, and give yourself a break that doesn’t depend on enforcing childcare boundaries all week.

I hear what you're saying, and I know you're trying to help me avoid drama. But I talked to my cousin Elena this weekend—she's a licensed family therapist—and she was pretty direct. She said walking away from people who repeatedly violate your boundaries is the only truly healthy move. Staying and trying to enforce boundaries with people who ignore them just teaches them that your limits are negotiable. So I'm struggling to see how going, even with boundaries stated upfront, isn't just setting myself up for the same dynamic.

Your concern about repeating last summer is grounded in something concrete: this year’s schedule again assigns you childcare without your agreement. Given how much last year affected you and how little capacity you feel for enforcing limits all week, **I still recommend sitting this trip out.**

But I wouldn’t endorse Elena’s broader claim that walking away is the *only* healthy response. Her credentials don’t make that absolute conclusion established. Attending with explicitly agreed limits—and acting if those limits are crossed—doesn’t inherently teach people that boundaries are negotiable. Whether that works depends on their behavior, your options, and the effort it requires from you.

The important distinction is between **“going could be workable under some circumstances”** and **“going is a good choice for you this year.”** The first can be true without the second being true. You don’t need to establish that going would be unhealthy for anyone in your position to decide that it asks too much of you.

You can tell Alex:

> “I understand why you think upfront boundaries could help. But last summer left me feeling used and invisible, and I don’t have the capacity to spend this vacation enforcing childcare limits. I’m sitting this year out. I’m not asking you to agree that boundaries could never work; I’m asking you to respect my decision about this trip.”

**Skip this year’s trip, handle any rental obligations separately, and leave broader decisions about family contact for another time.** Declining one vacation doesn’t require a verdict on every relationship involved.

I hear you. But I keep circling back to the same thing. If I go, I'm putting myself in a position where I have to enforce boundaries all week with people who've already shown they won't respect them. That's not a vacation. That's a job. And I'm not sure I have it in me.

Having to stay on guard against being assigned childcare would defeat what you need from a vacation. You’ve already described how much last summer hurt, and you don’t feel you have the capacity to risk another week like it.

You can’t know for certain how everyone would respond this year, but **you don’t have to test that by attending**. The current schedule already repeats the assumption that you’ll babysit. That, together with the cost to you, is enough reason to decline—not proof that withdrawing is the only healthy response, but a solid basis for your decision.

If you’re ready to decide, you can say:

> “I’ve decided to sit out the lake house trip this year. Last summer was difficult for me, and I need a vacation that doesn’t involve childcare responsibilities or managing expectations around them. Please plan without me. I’ll sort out any existing rental obligations separately.”

**My recommendation remains to skip this year’s trip.** You don’t need to join tonight’s call to defend that decision; a clear message beforehand is enough to communicate it.
I think I’ve decided. I’m going to text the group chat now and tell them I’m out for this year. I’ll handle the deposit separately.

That’s a clear decision that takes your limits seriously, and handling the deposit separately keeps the practical issue distinct.

You could send:

> “Hi everyone—I’ve decided not to join the lake house trip this year. Last summer was difficult for me, and I need a different kind of break this year. Please take me off the schedule and arrange childcare without me. I’ll handle the deposit separately. I won’t be joining tonight’s planning call.”

If anyone pushes for a debate: “I understand this changes the plans, but I’ve made my decision for this year.”

My recommendation is to keep the message brief, then mute the chat for the evening if you need some space.
